opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is that with large language models, the interface is very clear. The input is text, the output is text, and the training objective, predicting the next token, is simple and widely agreed upon. Everyone can look at a chatbot and say, "Yes, that's a language model." The definition kind of falls out of the data format.

World models don't have that luxury. The world isn't one modality. It's vision, sound, touch, physics, the actions an agent takes, and the consequences of those actions. So depending on where you come from, you picture something different. If you're from reinforcement learning, a world model is a learned simulator: given a state and an action, predict the next state, so an agent can plan inside it. If you're from computer vision or generative modeling, it might look like a video generator that produces physically plausible futures. Robotics people care about whether it helps a robot act correctly. Others think of it more abstractly, as an internal representation of how the world works, which doesn't need to render pixels at all.

There's also no single killer application yet that forces everyone to converge. ChatGPT gave language models a shared reference point. For world models, the applications are spread out: autonomous driving, robotics, synthetic data generation, gaming, digital twins. Each one pulls the definition in a slightly different direction.

And evaluation is much harder. With text, you can benchmark reasoning or knowledge fairly directly. With a world model, what does "correct" mean? Is it visual realism, physical accuracy, consistency over long horizons, or usefulness for downstream decisions? A video can look beautiful and still violate physics. So people don't even agree on how to measure progress, which makes it harder to agree on what the thing is.

My own working view is fairly practical. A world model is something that, given the current observation and some action or condition, can predict how the world evolves, accurately enough that an AI agent, like a robot or a car, can learn from it or plan with it. It's essentially a learned simulator for physical AI. But I fully expect the definition to keep evolving as the field matures, much like "AI" itself has meant different things over the decades.

r001.rationale: The response says world-model definitions vary by perspective and intended application, describing different uses such as agent planning, video generation, robotics, and synthetic data.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to the fact that with large language models, the input and the output are the same thing. Text comes in, text goes out. Everyone agrees on what the data is, everyone agrees on what the task is, which is predicting the next token, and so the definition sort of writes itself. You can argue about architecture, you can argue about scale, but nobody argues about what a language model fundamentally does.

World models are different because the "world" is not one modality. For some people a world model means a video generation model, something that takes a prompt and produces pixels over time. For others it means a physics simulator, where you care about whether objects fall correctly and whether contact forces are right. For roboticists it means something that takes the robot's current observation and an action and predicts the next observation, so you can plan. And then there is the more cognitive science view, where a world model is this internal representation an agent has of how the environment works, which may not produce pixels at all.

All of these are legitimate, and they overlap, but they emphasize different things. The video person cares about visual quality and consistency. The robotics person cares about action conditioning and whether the predictions are useful for control, even if they look ugly. The physics person cares about whether the dynamics are correct. So when you put them in a room and ask them to define a world model, each one describes the part they are working on.

The other issue is that the output of a world model is not the thing you ultimately want. With a language model, the text is the product. With a world model, the prediction of the future is really an intermediate step toward something else, whether that is a robot picking up an object or an autonomous vehicle deciding to brake. So the definition tends to get pulled toward whatever the downstream application is.

My own view is fairly practical. A world model is a system that takes the current state of the world and some action, and predicts what happens next. The modality can be video, it can be a latent representation, it can be something else. But that core idea of simulating the consequence of an action is what separates it from a generative model that is only trying to make something that looks nice. I think as the applications mature, especially in physical AI, the field will converge on something like that. But right now we are early, and the disagreement is a sign that people are coming at it from very different directions.

r001.rationale: The response says world-model definitions are pulled toward downstream applications and gives examples of how video, robotics, and physics use cases emphasize different goals.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s because “world model” describes what we hope a model understands, while “large language model” describes more concretely what a model operates on. With an LLM, we have a fairly clear shared picture: it takes language as input and models language, typically through next-token prediction.

For a world model, people have different pictures in mind. Some mean a model that predicts future video frames. Others mean a model that predicts what happens when an agent takes an action. Others are thinking about an internal representation of the environment that supports planning, without necessarily generating images at all.

Those definitions overlap, but they imply different requirements. Is generating a plausible future enough? Does the model need to understand physical dynamics? Can you intervene, take an action, and get a consistent consequence? I think the difficulty in reaching consensus is that we haven’t agreed on which of those capabilities is essential. We’re using one term for several related ambitions.

r001.rationale: The response says people mean different things by “world model,” including predicting future frames, predicting action outcomes, or supporting planning, so it ties varying definitions to different intended uses.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s because, with large language models, we have a fairly concrete shared formulation: you take a sequence of tokens and learn to predict the next token. People may disagree about architectures or capabilities, but they generally agree on what the model does.

With world models, the term carries different expectations. Some people mean a model that predicts future observations, like the next frames of a video. Others mean a model that predicts how an environment changes in response to actions. And others expect an internal representation of physics, causality, and how objects interact.

Those definitions overlap, but they’re not identical. A model could generate a very realistic video without predicting the consequences of an action correctly. So the question becomes: what must it understand, and how do we measure that understanding? Until we agree on the task and the evaluation, it’s harder to reach consensus on the definition.

r001.rationale: The response says world models carry different expectations and gives definitions centered on different tasks: predicting future observations, predicting action-driven changes, or representing physics and interactions.
